title: Praying for the dead
hookLine: many Christians pray for the dead; others entrust them to God

lines: IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT TO ASK?
cards: Carved at the bottom of an old headstone, under the name and dates, worn soft by rain: R.I.P. It can read like a goodbye. Sleep tight.
It's over now. But ask who those letters are talking to. Not the dead person, exactly, and not quite the people walking past.
Rest in peace is a request. Somebody is being asked to give that rest. The question under the stone: once someone has died, is there anything left to say to God about them?

teach.b: First, the words. R.I.P. stands for the Latin requiescat in pace, may he or she rest in peace: a prayer, shortened to fit on stone. Second, those who pray.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries, at Mass or the Divine Liturgy. An old Catholic prayer asks God to give them eternal rest and let perpetual light shine on them.
Orthodox services ask God to give rest to the soul of his servant, where there is no pain or sorrow.
They point to Second Maccabees, a book in their Bibles, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died, and the book praises praying for the dead.
And Paul writes of his friend Onesiphorus: "The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." Some readers think Onesiphorus had already died; the letter doesn't say.
Third, those who entrust. Protestants who follow the Reformers don't pray for the dead. They hold that a person who has died is already safe in God's hands, and nothing needs adding.

They can lean on Revelation: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." Rest, already given. So at the grave they give thanks, and let go.
Fourth, look at both: one keeps speaking to God about the person, one places the person in God's hands.
Both refuse to treat death as the end of God's care. Rest in peace can be either: a prayer, or a hand opening.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries of a death and in the Mass or Divine Liturgy; in Protestant churches that do not, the dead are commended to God and the service gives thanks for their life.

games.q: what does “praying for the dead” mean?
o: asking God to give rest to someone who has died
a prayer only a priest may say at a burial
trying to contact the dead and hear them reply

games.q: praying for the dead — tap the pairs.
p: may he or she rest in peace
an offering for soldiers who died
may he find mercy in that day

s: R.I.P. is just a polite goodbye
it shortens a Latin prayer, requiescat in pace: may he or she rest in peace.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at Mass and the Liturgy
they keep speaking to God about those who have died, at funerals, on anniversaries and in their services.
Christians who don't pray for the dead think God has stopped caring for them
they hold the dead are already safe in God's hands, so they entrust them and give thanks.

games.q: you're Paul, writing to Timothy. your friend Onesiphorus searched Rome for you and wasn't ashamed of your chains. what do you write about him?
o: a request: may he find mercy of the Lord in that day.
an order to Timothy to find him.
games.why: "the Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." some readers think Onesiphorus had died; the letter doesn't say.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you still carry, the way they stood or laughed.
If you pray for the dead, ask God to give them rest; if you entrust instead, place them in God's hands; if you don't pray, hold them in your thoughts, then open your hands a little.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Praying for the dead. Some Christians keep praying for those who have died; others entrust them to God and give thanks.

orig.note: Latin: may he or she rest in peace, shortened on headstones to R.I.P.

carryVoice: Your line: rest in peace. Three letters, and a request inside them. That's today, done.
